newsitem.title: USA: Palladium soars to record high on worsening supply headache.
newsitem.headline: Palladium soars to record high on worsening supply headache.

text.p: Palladium, a precious metal hidden in dental work or car exhaust sytems, Wednesday jumped to a record high as a strike at the world's largest producer in South Africa threatened to worsen an already bad supply headache.

June palladium was up $9.50 to $184.00 an ounce, the highest since last summer on the New York Mercantile Exchange after setting a record high of $188.00 on the London market, beating levels set in 1989.
Prices soared on news of a strike at Rustenburg, the world's largest platinum mine, in South Africa, following five months of delay in exports by Russia, the biggest supplier.
At the end of last year, palladium was holding at a stable $115 until prices flew up on a supply squeeze.
"The market has gone crazy. The market is very, very tight," said a dealer in London.
About 15 to 20 percent of production has been affected by Tuesday's wildcat strike at Anglo American Platinum Corp.'s Rustenburg operations.
"It takes really something special for palladium to be at over $180," said one analyst.
Palladium, which is part of the so-called platinum group metals, is used in electronics, chemical applications and catalysts that remove noxious gases from car exhausts.
Platinum also rode on palladium's coattails, gaining $1.50 to $398.50 an ounce on the NYMEX after rising to $404.50 in London, matching its recent high of Aug. 1, 1996.

Only rarely does palladium emerge from the shadow of more glamorous gold, silver and platinum, as it did in 1989, when it was used in experiments that briefly seemed to herald a new "Cold Fusion" energy source. But the price collapsed when further research failed to support initial results.

Trading in palladium and platinum has always been a low-key business compared to that in gold. Gold has been hoarded by governments and individuals as a store of value for centuries, and almost every ton of it ever mined is still being stored somewhere on the planet.
In contrast, platinum and palladium have always gone straight to industry or jewellery, except for a small tonnage held mainly in Japan, where investors buy platinum bars.

The rare white metals soared at the end of the 1970s, when gold and silver reached historic highs on inflation fears after the Organisation of the Petroleum Exporting Countries lifted the cost of oil to $40 a barrel. Platinum reached its highest price of about $1,050 in early March 1980 and palladium peaked at $335.00.
Since the official fixings began, palladium's top price was $181.50 in 1989, when laboratory tests suggested that "Cold Fusion" might work, creating a new demand for the metal.
In April 1995, another new application for palladium was briefly in the spotlight and prices raced upward again.
